name: move the shorter wall
hook: Two pointers on an array that isn't sorted. It still works, and the reason is the part interviewers push on.
hook_sub: Container With Most Water, and why moving the shorter wall is safe.
caption: Pick two lines. The water they hold is the distance between them times the shorter line's height. Find the most.
Every pair of {n} lines is {pairs} containers. Start with the widest container instead and move the shorter wall inward: {steps} containers measured, same answer.

The rule is easy to guess and hard to prove. Here is the proof: keep the shorter wall and narrow, and the width shrinks while the height is still capped by that wall. It can never win. So one measurement speaks for every container that wall could form, and the wall is discarded.
The input isn't sorted, and sorting would destroy the widths. What makes the elimination work this time is the width shrinking with every move.
Could you have proved it in an interview? 👇
cta: Next in the module: Trapping Rain Water.

p: Area is the distance between two lines times the *shorter* line's height.

slides.h: Start widest. Move the shorter wall.

p: Keep the shorter wall and narrow: the width shrinks, and the height is still capped by that wall. It can never win.

rows.lab: Best of every container that uses line 0

p: Sorting would destroy the widths, so sortedness can't be the reason.
The width shrinks with every move, so the only hope of improvement is a taller minimum, and the shorter wall is the one holding it down.
That is what lets *one measurement speak for a whole family*.
